By ascertaining the three <term>vajras</term> <gloss>indestructible realities of body, speech, and mind</gloss> and definitively realizing selflessness, one completely severs the delusions of existence. When that very reality becomes one's own mantra, it is easy to find the perfect method. For such a <term>Vajra-holder</term> <gloss>tantric adept</gloss>, the <term>siddhi</term> <gloss>attainment</gloss> resides in the very palm of their hand. This is what is taught by such passages.

Therefore, this is not an insignificant matter. For this reason, at the very moment of the fourth empowerment, those sentient beings with the sharpest faculties will achieve the attainment of <term>Mahamudra</term> <gloss>the Great Seal of reality</gloss>. Furthermore, for others who are different from them, the oral instructions of the Great Seal should be shown.

Now, with the phrase, "the nature of wisdom is <term>Lalana</term>," and so forth, the distinction of the three channels will be shown in order to thoroughly establish the meaning of empowerment. <term>Lalana</term> is the left channel; it is the nature of the <term>ali</term> <gloss>vowels</gloss> and the essence of wisdom. <term>Rasana</term> is the right channel; it is the nature of the <term>kali</term> <gloss>consonants</gloss> and the essence of method. That which resides in the central region as the essence of their unity is <term>Avadhuti</term>. <term>Lalana</term> is the <term>Dharmakaya</term> <gloss>Truth Body</gloss>. <term>Rasana</term> is the <term>Sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>Enjoyment Body</gloss>. <term>Avadhuti</term> is the <term>Nirmanakaya</term> <gloss>Emanation Body</gloss>. These correspond respectively to body, speech, and mind. From joining the three chakras non-dually with the three channels, Great Bliss will arise.

If Great Bliss is realized, the distinctions of the four empowerments, the moments, and the joys will also become known as pure awareness itself. Just as the sequential arrangement of the number of chakras is established for the generation stage, it should be understood similarly for the empowerment stage.

Regarding the four noble truths and so forth, they also correspond sequentially to the four empowerments. They are the purifications of: fully knowing suffering, abandoning the origin, manifesting cessation, and meditating on the path. Likewise, reality is fourfold. As for the reality of the self: briefly stated, the five aggregates are well known as the five Buddhas. The <term>vajra</term> sense sources are themselves the <term>mandala</term> of the <term>Vajra Dakinis</term>. Thus it was said. Regarding the reality of the deity and so forth, in the <term>Hevajra</term> <note>original: "Dgyes pa'i"</note> <unclear>one or two words unread</unclear>

<summary>This page explains the internal anatomy of the subtle body, mapping the three channels to the three bodies of a Buddha and the four empowerments to the Four Noble Truths. It emphasizes that realization of Great Bliss leads to the attainment of Mahamudra.</summary>
<keywords>Lalana, Rasana, Avadhuti, three channels, four empowerments, Great Bliss, Mahamudra, four noble truths, subtle body, five Buddhas</keywords>

On the sixteen petals,
The <term>Sambhogacakra</term> <gloss>Wheel of Enjoyment</gloss> resides.
The syllable <term>Ya</term> is shown as the element of wind.
The <term>Samayamudra</term> <gloss>Commitment Gesture</gloss> is the goddess Tara <note>Literally "She who Delivers"</note>.
On the thirty-two petals of the lotus,
The <term>Mahasukha-cakra</term> <gloss>Wheel of Great Bliss</gloss> resides.
Listening is explained as being <term>Sahaja</term> <gloss>Co-emergent</gloss>.
One should distinguish between them through a two-fold division.

The yoga of conventional deities
Belongs to the side of the <term>Utpatti-krama</term> <gloss>Generation Stage</gloss>.
That which has the form of bliss free from obscuration
Is the meditation of the <term>Sampanna-krama</term> <gloss>Completion Stage</gloss>.
The teachings of the Dharma by the Buddhas
Completely rely upon the two truths.
As it has been stated elsewhere:
By relying on these two stages,
Namely the side of the Generation Stage
And that of the Completion Stage,
<term>Vajradhara</term> <gloss>The Vajra Holder</gloss> reveals the teachings.
Because of that statement, the previous explanation of the phrase "Thus have I heard at one time" applies here. In that setting, the <term>Bhagavan</term> <gloss>Blessed One</gloss> spoke to the assembly.
If one asks what kind of special quality this has:
It is the essence of the body, speech, and mind of all the <term>Tathagatas</term> <gloss>Thus-Gone Ones</gloss>; it is the deity who has become the very vital nectar.
For that reason, the secret of all the Tathagatas is Vajradhara.
Even more secret than that is <term>Karuna-vajra</term> <gloss>Compassion Vajra</gloss>, which is not to be revealed to <term>Sravakas</term> <gloss>Foundational Hearers</gloss> and the like.
Then, realizing that this is difficult to find, the assembly became filled with faith and enthusiasm. To further inspire them, the Bhagavan spoke the words: "O, <term>Vajragarbha</term> <gloss>Vajra Essence</gloss>," and so forth.
The command "Listen!" refers to the application of hearing.
When it says "Vajragarbha requested," what did he request?
He requested to ask about three specific meanings.
The Bhagavan replied: "The Vajra is said to be indivisible," and so forth.
It is indivisible because it cannot be separated; it cannot be harmed by the arguments of oneself or others.
If one asks what that is, it is the <term>Dharma</term>...

<summary>This page explains the tantric anatomy of the energy wheels and the necessity of the two stages of meditation. It identifies Vajradhara as the source of secret teachings and introduces the dialogue between the Buddha and Vajragarbha.</summary>
<keywords>Sambhogacakra, Mahasukhacakra, Generation Stage, Completion Stage, Vajradhara, Vajragarbha, Indivisible Vajra</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical commentary on the Hevajra Tantra, specifically focusing on the internal yogic process of the inner heat and the dissolution of the aggregates into luminosity.</meta>

Regarding the phrase **Blazing at the navel**: here, the word **navel** <note>original: "pīṭha" or "nābhi"</note> refers to the center, meaning the <term>Avadhūti</term> <gloss>central channel</gloss> situated between the left and right channels.

The phrase **Burnt** refers to the five <term>skandhas</term> <gloss>aggregates of personality</gloss> being consumed by the fire of great passion.

The phrase **Locanā and the others** refers to the elements such as earth and so forth.

The phrase **Having been burnt** refers to the burning away of the notions of "I" and "mine" <note>the ego and its attachments</note>.

The phrase **The Moon-holder <term>Haṃ</term> drips** refers to the arising of the pristine wisdom of great bliss. This will be explained further:

->The Co-emergent is not described by others,<-
->And it is not found anywhere else.<-
->Through the instruction on the Master's timing,<-
->One knows it oneself through merit.<-

This is an explanation of the perfect realization. <term>Caṇḍā</term> <gloss>fierce woman</gloss> is wisdom <note>prajñā</note>; she practices the meditative absorption of the generation and completion stages. <term>Āli</term> is the mind whose nature is great compassion. Therefore, emptiness and compassion are expressed by the term <term>Caṇḍālī</term> <gloss>inner heat yoga</gloss>. 

The **navel** is the center of these two, characterized by the luminosity of the <term>Mahāmudrā</term> <gloss>Great Seal</gloss>. At that location, the inner heat is kindled, which is the unsurpassed wisdom. What does it do? It is said, **The five Tathāgatas and so forth**, meaning Akṣobhya and the others who are the lords of the mandala and the mandala deities, as well as Locanā and the rest.

**Burnt** means that not even a trace of ash remains. Then, having been burnt, the phrase **Moon-holder <term>Haṃ</term>** means that because there is nothing other than the mental elaborations of "I" and "mine," the "self" is simply the mind itself <note>cittamātra</note>. 

If one asks what occurs through the burning: the text says, **The Moon-holder drips**. Therefore, after arising from the meditative absorption of luminosity, the "Moon-holder" remains as Vajradhara <note>the Holder of the Thunderbolt</note>. As it is said:

->The past and the future,<-
->And the present are the three worlds.<-
->Through the purity of luminosity,<-
->All are seen in that single moment.<-

In the title **Chapter of the Vajra Family**, **Vajra** here refers to Hevajra. **Family** <note>original: "kula"</note> refers to the body. Alternatively, that which arises from it is the family. The chapter that makes this manifest is the **Chapter of the Vajra Family**. This concludes the difficult points of the Hevajra... <unclear>one or two syllables obscured</unclear>

<summary>The text explains the yogic symbolism of Caṇḍālī or inner heat, where the fire of wisdom consumes the ego and the five aggregates, leading to the dripping of bliss from the crown and the realization of luminosity.</summary>
<keywords>Caṇḍālī, inner heat, Avadhūti, Hevajra, luminosity, five aggregates, Vajradhara, Co-emergent wisdom</keywords>

<meta>continues from the previous page concerning the ritual applications of mantras and visualization</meta>

One should first recite the mantra <term>Om Hum Svaha</term> one hundred thousand times for the purpose of the preliminary service <gloss>the initial retreat or accumulation required to empower a mantra</gloss>. Subsequently, one should write the syllable <term>Pam</term> using <term>steatite</term> <gloss>soapstone or lithomarge</gloss> on an unbaked earthen vessel. In the center of that, one should write: <term>Om Hum Devadatta Stambhaya Hum Svaha</term> <note>Devadatta is used here as a placeholder name for the target of the ritual; Stambhaya means to paralyze or suppress</note>. Having filled the vessel with ashes from a cemetery, cover it with another new unbaked earthen vessel so that their mouths are joined. 

Upon the top, draw a four-sided <term>mandala</term> <gloss>sacred geometric circle</gloss> of the Great Powerful One <note>Mahabala</note>, beautifully adorned with <term>vajras</term> <gloss>ritual scepters symbolizing indestructibility</gloss>. Place this underground and press down upon it with the left foot. While remaining in meditative absorption as previously explained, recite the mantra. If one recites <term>Om Hum Vajra Devadatta Stambhaya Hum Svaha</term> one hundred and eight or one thousand times, the target will be paralyzed.

Similarly, one should perform the yoga of the White Goddess <note>Gauri</note>, who is saffron-colored and completely perfect, arising from the syllable <term>I</term>. She holds a noose and an iron hook. 

Meditate on the syllable <term>Am</term> in one's own heart, colored like a <term>Bandhuka</term> flower <gloss>a bright red species, Pentapetes phoenicea</gloss>. For the purpose of the preliminary service, recite the mantra <term>Om Am Svaha</term> one hundred thousand times. Then, visualize the person to be accomplished <gloss>the target of the ritual</gloss> in front of oneself, red in color, stripped of clothing, and with hair loosened. In their <term>bhaga</term> <gloss>secret place or womb</gloss>, imagine the syllable <term>Om</term> with the color of fire. Alternatively, if it is a man, imagine it in the heart. 

Contemplate that they are melted and intoxicated by the light of the syllable <term>Am</term>. Recite <term>Om Am Gauri [Name] Me Vashamanaya Hum Svaha</term> <note>Vashamanaya means to bring under one's control or power</note>. Visualize binding their throat with the noose and piercing their heart with the iron hook. If one contemplates drawing them perfectly until they arrive at the soles of one's feet, they will certainly be brought under one's power.

Similarly, visualize the yogini of the Water Element <note>Chu ma</note>, blue in color and completely perfect, arising from the syllable <term>I</term>. Her hands are in the gesture of the thumb and index finger touching. In the heart, imagine a blue syllable <term>Kham</term> upon a sun disk. For the purpose of the preliminary service, first recite <term>Om Kham Svaha</term> one hundred thousand times. 

Then, visualize the person to be accomplished stripped of clothes, with hair disheveled, and riding a blue camel. Imagine them facing the southern direction, fleeing in a state of agitation while being struck by a figure brandishing a wooden staff. Recite the mantra: <term>Om A Kham Vira Yogini [Name] Uccataya Kham Hum Hum Hum Phat</term> <note>Uccataya means to drive away or expel</note>. Within seven days, they will certainly be expelled. 

Similarly, from the syllable <term>U</term>, the <term>Vajra Dakini</term> <gloss>Vajra Sky-Goer</gloss>...

<summary>This page details specific tantric rituals for paralyzing enemies, subjugating individuals through the yoga of Gauri, and expelling targets using the blue yogini and the Uccataya mantra.</summary>
<keywords>Mantra, preliminary service, Stambhana, Vashikarana, Uccatana, Gauri, Yogini, ritual visualization, Derge Tengyur</keywords>

It is called the Being <term>Sattva</term> <gloss>a heroic or enlightened being</gloss>. This means that the seed syllable itself is <term>Vajradhara</term> <gloss>the Bearer of the Vajra, the primordial Buddha</gloss>. If one asks what his special quality is, he is described as having a nature of supreme bliss. Regarding the phrase "radiating outward," this means that from that very seed syllable, one should radiate various forms identical to the body of <term>Hevajra</term> <gloss>Joyful Vajra</gloss> until they pervade everything. Regarding "gathering them back into the heart," it means that those same forms are thoroughly reabsorbed and dissolved back into that very seed syllable. 

Then the yogi, having become the essence of wrath <note>referring to the transformation of ordinary anger into enlightened fury</note>, arises in the form of <term>Heruka</term> <gloss>a wrathful semi-出場 deity</gloss> from the total transformation of the moon, the sun, the hand-symbol, and the seed syllable. These are the five aspects of manifest enlightenment <term>abhisambodhi</term>. As it is stated in the eighth chapter:

The moon is the mirror-like wisdom.
The seventh of the seventh <note>referring to the sun disk</note> is the wisdom of equality.
The seed syllable and the hand-symbol of the deity
Are described as the wisdom of discernment.
Their total unification is the wisdom of perseverance,
And their perfection is the pure sphere of reality <term>dharmadhatu</term>.

The phrases beginning with "blue" and "sun" refer to these three as the yoga of the solitary hero, which is common to all deities. 

Now, in order to briefly show the four types of Hevajra and the fourth yoga of <term>Nairatmya</term> <gloss>Lady of Egolessness</gloss> which consists of the mandala circle, the text mentions "the charnel ground" and so forth. The activities of the fourth yoga should be viewed in the same way as the third yoga. Inside the vajra fence, within the celestial palace of the mandala of the eight terrifying charnel grounds, the Lord Hevajra is completely surrounded by the eight yoginis such as <term>Gauri</term> and the others. 

The phrase "where the breath moves" is an explanation of the word <term>shmashana</term> <gloss>charnel ground</gloss> by removing certain letters of the etymology <note>the author is providing a tantric etymology linking the word for charnel ground to the resting place of the body or breath</note>. It means the "abode of the corpse." This brief teaching on the charnel ground will also be perfected in the eighth chapter which is to be explained later. "Charnel ground" means that in the body, which is without a self, the Lord resides in a nature of supreme bliss. If one asks how the body is a charnel ground, it is said: "By this logic of where the breath moves, it is called a charnel ground." Now, to specifically describe the four-armed Hevajra—

<summary>This page explains the visualization process of Hevajra through the five aspects of enlightenment and provides a tantric etymology of the charnel ground as the human body.</summary>
<keywords>Hevajra, Heruka, Five Wisdoms, abhisambodhi, charnel ground, Nairatmya, seed syllable, Vajradhara</keywords>

The practicing yogi should not become intoxicated <note>refers to the avoidance of mental dullness or physical intoxication</note>, as the predominance of delusion becomes a great obstacle to yoga; thus, one should train in this manner. This concludes the commentary on the sixth chapter, the Chapter on Conduct, from the *Jeweled Garland: A Commentary on the Difficult Points of the Hevajra Tantra* <note>original: "Dgyes pa'i rdo rje'i dka' 'grel rnal 'byor rin po che'i phreng ba"</note>.

Signs <note>term: <term>sandhyā-bhāṣā</term> <gloss>twilight language or symbolic gestures</gloss></note> are the language of the <term>Mlecchas</term> <gloss>barbarians or outsiders</gloss>, used by the <term>yoginīs</term> <gloss>female practitioners</gloss> to demonstrate their realization. Furthermore, one should understand that this is the supreme method itself. Therefore, the "Chapter on Signs" and so forth was spoken. In the chapter clarifying signs, it says the following:

"Brother" refers to the <term>yogī</term> <gloss>male practitioner</gloss>.
"Sister" refers to the <term>yoginī</term> <gloss>female practitioner</gloss>.

Regarding the phrase "one finger," it refers to the index finger, meaning "Have you come?"
Regarding "which one," it means which one should look.
Regarding "with two," it refers to the index and middle fingers together.
"Showing the silk scarf" means showing the manner of binding a silk scarf with those two fingers.
"Three points" refers to pressing the pinky finger with the thumb and extending the remaining three fingers in the manner of three points.
"The boundary" refers to the boundary at the crown of the head.
"The wheel" refers to showing the form of a wheel.
"Frowning" refers to the movement of the eyebrows.
"Loosening the topknot" and so forth are explanations of the provisional meaning <note>interpretations meant to guide the practitioner toward deeper truths</note>.

Regarding "one finger is shown," and so forth: showing either one finger—the index finger—or both the middle and index fingers toward the lotus <note>metaphor for the female consort's secret organ</note> of wisdom <term>prajñā</term> acts as an exhortation.
Regarding "that itself is the 'well-come,'" "well" <note>original: "legs par"</note> refers to the fluid <note>seminal or vital essence</note>, meaning it was brought down through the joining of the fingers.

Regarding the "mudrā of illness" and so forth: the "mudrā of illness" is the realization of the <term>dharmadhātu</term> <gloss>sphere of reality</gloss>, which is the ultimate limit of bliss; these things are to be known.
If one asks what that is like: "From grasping the left thumb" and so forth was spoken. "Left" refers to wisdom <term>prajñā</term>, meaning the interior of her lotus. The "thumb" is the <term>vajra</term> <gloss>the male organ or diamond-bolt</gloss>; when it reaches the state of emission, it is to be pressed.
Regarding "the ring finger" and so forth: the ring finger refers to the wisdom of primordial awareness <term>jñāna</term>.

<summary>This page provides a technical commentary on the symbolic hand gestures and coded language used between tantric practitioners to communicate spiritual realization and ritual intent. It interprets specific physical signs as metaphors for internal yogic states and the union of wisdom and method.</summary>
<keywords>Hevajra Tantra, yogini, mudra, twilight language, prajna, vajra, symbolic gestures, tantric conduct</keywords>

The lotus of <note>the female consort</note>. Wisdom <note>original: "prajña"</note> refers to the <term>vajra</term> <gloss>the diamond-like male organ or principle</gloss>. Meditation refers to the process of entering into union. These three elements occur first, while the two forms of the co-emergent are at the end; that which is to be meditated upon lies between these two. The act of meditative stabilization is called <term>samapatti</term> <gloss>equipoise or union</gloss>. The bliss arising from the cultivation and generation of that state is called "its bliss."

The term wheel <note>original: "cakra"</note> refers to the wheel of the <term>yogini</term> <gloss>female tantric practitioner</gloss>, because they are all gathered within that very great bliss. What is the nature of that bliss? It is described as being "as is appropriate." Self-cognition <note>original: "svasamvedana"</note> means the essence of knowing by oneself, without depending on external conditions. That very self-cognition is enlightenment <note>original: "bodhi"</note>. The mind that has the nature of enlightenment is called the <term>bodhicitta</term> <gloss>enlightened mind or vital essence</gloss>. The word "activity" has the sense of gathering or encompassing. Because it causes the body to remain, it is called the deity.

The phrase "as it arises" means arising according to the actual nature of reality; it is how things arise without depending on the duality of subject and object. The fluid <note>original: "shukra"</note> takes the form of fluid like a jasmine flower or the moon. Why is this so? It is said: "The co-emergent is of two kinds." This refers to the two types of co-emergent joy.

If the co-emergent is like that, then what are "man" and "woman"? The text speaks of "the consort" and so on. Regarding these, there are seven elements and two types of joy. What are they? They are the relative <note>original: "samvriti"</note> and the ultimate <note>original: "paramartha"</note>. The essence of great bliss is the ultimate. That which arises according to appearances is the relative, because it possesses the portion of the relative itself. For that very reason, there are two types.

Regarding the word "four," it refers to the four joys. The "distinction" refers to the general distinctions of the co-emergent. One might ask: "Is it not usually asserted that there are four joys? Does the different assertion here not become a contradiction?" To this, the text says: "In this way, the co-emergent..." and so forth. It means they arise through the sequence of the four, such as joy, supreme joy, and so on, according to the stage of generation <note>original: "utpattikrama"</note>.

<summary>This page provides a tantric commentary on the nature of great bliss, defining terms like wisdom, the co-emergent, and the two levels of truth—relative and ultimate—within the context of meditative union. It clarifies how the sequence of the four joys relates to the generation stage of practice.</summary>
<keywords>co-emergent, great bliss, bodhicitta, four joys, relative truth, ultimate truth, tantric physiology, yoga</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the nature of the six faculties and the practice of Great Seal meditation.</meta>

The six faculties refer to those residing in the body, such as the eyes and so forth. Regarding the terms stationary <note>original: བརྟེན་ or བརྟན་</note> and moving, these refer to external objects that possess mind <note>sentient beings</note> and those that are inanimate. The phrase "I myself am" indicates that not only is the self alone the Vajra Holder <term>Vajradhara</term> <gloss>the primordial Buddha representing the ultimate state of enlightenment</gloss> by nature of great bliss.

Equalness and similarity mean being in the state of indivisible essence. If one asks what that is like, the text says, "by meditating on thatness." The explanation for this is called "equal taste" <term>samarasa</term> <gloss>the meditative experience where all dualities and phenomena are perceived as having the same essence of bliss and emptiness</gloss>. Furthermore, the explanation of this equality and so forth means the meaning of becoming similar. The term "that" refers to the inferior, the mediocre, and so forth. The term "taste" refers to the essence, which is a synonym for "entity." If one asks what the taste is, it refers to the innate nature characterized by great bliss atop the chakra. To show the summarized meaning, it is said:

->Meditation is the equality of a single taste.<-

Furthermore, if one asks how to meditate on the equality of a single taste, the text says "from me" and so forth. "The yogi, having known it thus" means having grasped it with certainty. "Deeply composed in meditative absorption" means at all times and in all states. To clarify that point, the text mentions "eating and drinking" and so forth. "By nature" means engaging by its own natural state. Regarding the phrase "Great Seal" <term>Mahamudra</term> <gloss>the highest meditative teaching in the Tibetan tradition, focusing on the direct realization of the nature of mind</gloss> and so forth, it means "for the sake of accomplishing the Great Seal." This demonstrates the yoga of superior devotion.

Now, to show the mind within this very context, the text says "all beings will become meditation" and so forth. "All beings" refers to sentient beings and the vessel-like world <note>the physical universe</note>; all of these arise precisely from meditation. If one asks why, it says "by the mind," meaning by the conceptual consciousness. If one thinks that if things are not examined, they will not become meditation, the text says "all phenomena" and so forth, meaning the complete knowledge of the innate essence.

<summary>This page explains the concept of "equal taste" in meditation, where all phenomena are realized as the essence of great bliss. It describes how a yogi maintains this awareness of the Great Seal throughout all daily activities including eating and drinking.</summary>
<keywords>equal taste, samarasa, Great Seal, Mahamudra, Vajradhara, chakra, innate nature, meditation, conceptual consciousness</keywords>

<meta>The text provides a commentary on the Hevajra Tantra, specifically discussing the realization of ultimate reality and the nature of the deity Vajrasattva.</meta>

The mantra is <term>om ah hum phat svaha</term>. Offering and making requests refers to the Guru. The phrase as it has been explained refers to texts such as the <term>Tattvasamgraha</term> <gloss>Compendium of Reality</gloss>. <term>Vajrasattva</term> <gloss>Adamantine Being</gloss> refers to <term>Hevajra</term>. The term afterwards refers to the period immediately following the initiation. Complete purity refers to the purification of the stains of cyclic existence. One possessed of the form of wisdom refers to being equal to omniscient wisdom.

Regarding the phrase cyclic existence and complete purification, it means that for this wisdom, there is not even the slightest difference between existence and nirvana. This is superior because it is completely beyond all conceptual elaboration. This very point will be clearly shown by the two verses beginning with supreme joy.

Supreme joy refers to supreme wisdom, which is the wisdom characterized by clear light. The phrase there is no meditation means there is nothing whatsoever to be meditated upon. The meditator is the mind, and that too does not exist. The body is the physical body. The apprehended refers to entities that appear. The apprehender refers to the sense faculties such as the eyes. Likewise, flesh, blood, and so forth also do not exist.

Thus, having established that the obscuration of afflictions does not exist, the text says there is no seeing and so forth to demonstrate that the obscuration to knowledge also does not exist. This means that external entities to be seen and so forth do not exist.

Regarding the phrase without waves, waves refer to conceptual thoughts. Their exhaustion is what is meant by being without waves. Diversity refers to the appearance of various forms. Its absence is the lack of diversity. The phrase thus spoken refers to these words spoken by the Lord <note>original: Bhagavan</note>. The word requested refers to the questions asked by <term>Vajragarbha</term>. To the question of what was requested, the text says why and so forth. The intention is this: by the very nature of the Sahaja <gloss>Co-emergent</gloss> essence, all is naturally pure.

<summary>This page provides a philosophical commentary on the Hevajra Tantra, explaining the non-duality of existence and nirvana through the lens of primordial purity and the absence of a meditating subject or object.</summary>
<keywords>Hevajra, Vajrasattva, Vajragarbha, non-duality, clear light, emptiness, Sahaja, Tattvasamgraha</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>the purity of the hands is described. The reality of the sixteen hands is the sixteen types of emptiness, which are as follows:

the emptiness of the internal,
the emptiness of the external,
the emptiness of both the internal and external,
the emptiness of the great,
the emptiness of emptiness,
the emptiness of the ultimate,
the emptiness of the conditioned,
the emptiness of the unconditioned,
the emptiness of that which transcends limits,
the emptiness of that without beginning or end,
the emptiness of that which is not cast aside,
the emptiness of nature,
the emptiness of specific characteristics,
the emptiness of all phenomena,
the emptiness of non-entities, and
the emptiness of the essence of non-entities.

These sixteen are indeed represented as the hands. The feet represent the purity that conquers the <term>maras</term> <gloss>demonic obstructions</gloss>, namely: the <term>mara</term> of the aggregates, the <term>mara</term> of afflictions, the <term>mara</term> of the lord of death, and the <term>mara</term> of the son of the gods.

Regarding the phrase "the faces," it refers to the actual faces of the deity. The "three vajras" refer to the <term>vajra</term> <gloss>indestructible</gloss> body, speech, and mind. There is no cessation even at the time when things do not appear. Although they may become one, there is no decrease, and although they may become many, there is no increase. Within these, there is not even a slight degree of <term>klesha</term> <gloss>affliction or mental defilement</gloss> or <term>vyavadana</term> <gloss>purification</gloss>. In that same way, because the <term>parikalpita-svabhava</term> <gloss>the imagined or imputed nature</gloss> is utterly non-existent, there is no arising and no cessation. There is no increase, no decrease, no affliction, and no purification.

Enlightenment as well is the <term>parinispanna-svabhava</term> <gloss>the thoroughly established or perfected nature</gloss>. Because it is utterly secluded, transcending all conceptual construction, and is like space, it has no arising and no cessation. It has no increase and no decrease. Because it is utterly pure by its very nature, there is no affliction. Because it is pure by its own essence, there is no purification.

If one asks why this is so, it is shown through statements such as "form is like an illusion" and "feeling is like an illusion." This is further demonstrated in two ways: through the non-existence of the illusion itself and through the non-existence of the consciousness that grasps at the illusion. An illusion is merely a name; it does not abide in an object and it does not abide in a direction. By saying this, it is shown that because the illusion is an imagined construct, it does not truly exist.

The statement "seeing an illusion is an error; it does not exist" shows that consciousness itself does not truly exist <note>referring to consciousness as a substantial, independent entity</note>. In this context, the phrase "it does not abide in an object" shows that the illusion does not have the characteristics of physical matter. This is because material phenomena do not abide in an object <note>in the sense of being independent of the mind's imputation</note>. 

The phrase "it does not abide in a direction" shows that it does not have the characteristics of the formless. Although phenomena with formless characteristics, such as consciousness, do not abide in an object, they are designated as abiding in a direction, such as the direction of the eye and so forth. Therefore, they are said to "abide in a direction." The term "error" <note>original: "log par gyur pa"</note> shows that it is not the truth. The term "does not exist" shows the characteristic of the absence of a thing <note>original: "dngos po med pa", referring to the lack of an ontological essence or bhava</note>.

The phrase "devoid of intrinsic nature" <note>original: "ngo bo nyid dang bral ba"</note> demonstrates the absence of any inherent essence. A Bodhisattva <gloss>a being dedicated to awakening</gloss> is described as "perceiving in a dream-like manner." This refers to how a Bodhisattva, a Great Being, practices the Perfection of Wisdom. At that time, they do not truly perceive the arising of any phenomena.

Regarding the Three Natures:
First, in the <term>imagined nature</term> <gloss>parikalpita</gloss>, there is neither arising nor ceasing; there is only appearance and non-appearance.
Second, in the <term>dependent nature</term> <gloss>paratantra</gloss>, there is neither increase nor decrease; it is merely the imagined aspect.
Third, in the <term>perfected nature</term> <gloss>parinispanna</gloss>, there is neither affliction nor purification; it is simply naturally pure by its very essence.

Although all phenomena are thus without intrinsic nature, in order to clear away further doubts, one might ask: why is this so? It is because names are merely artificial constructions. The names and signs for the aggregates <gloss>skandhas</gloss> such as "form," "feeling," and "perception" are artificial. They do not exist by way of their own intrinsic nature. Therefore, one should understand that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, because an intrinsic nature is not something that can be artificially constructed.

That which is artificial is taught through the statement: "these phenomena which arise dependently are conceptualized." This means that based on conceptual causes and conceptual conditions, various phenomena are designated as "dependently originated."

This demonstrates the following point: if something depends on another, those phenomena arise through the power of something else and not through their own power. If so, how could they possess an intrinsic nature? Therefore, since they lack their own entity and exist as the entity of another, it is established that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. Consequently, the meaning of "lacking intrinsic nature" is the same as the meaning of "dependent origination." Following this, the conventional use of names arises from the causes of imagined names.

Regarding the statement that the meaning of the word <term>Bodhisattva</term> <gloss>enlightenment hero</gloss> is a meaning without a basis: there are four aspects of meaning for Bodhisattvas. Through this mental engagement, sentient beings are categorized into the three groups <note>the groups of those certain of the right path, those certain of the wrong path, and those whose path is not yet determined</note>. Regarding the passage beginning with, "Blessed One, how can a Tathagata <gloss>One Gone to Thusness</gloss>, an Arhat <gloss>Worthy One</gloss>, a perfectly completed Buddha..." the Elder <note>referring to Subhuti</note> asked: "If meditative concentrations, clairvoyant powers, and sentient beings are all of an essence lacking inherent existence, how are they produced? To this, the Blessed One replied with the passage beginning, "Subhuti, if desires and sinful, unwholesome factors..." demonstrating that because things are of an essence lacking inherent existence, everything is possible; otherwise, it would not be so. These marks are presented through four aspects: the brief summary, the detailed explanation, the cause, and the result.

First is the brief summary. After that, the commentary on those marks is the detailed explanation. Mentioning the past actions <note>original: "karma"</note> is the cause. Mentioning the preliminary signs is the result.

Regarding the phrase, "Possessing the mark of a wheel on the palms and soles," there are two types of wheels in the world: the wheel used as a weapon and the wheel used for movement, such as the wheel of a chariot. These marks appear on both the hands and the feet.

The past actions leading to this are also of two types. First are those subsumed under the <term>Paramita</term> <gloss>Perfection</gloss> of Ethics <note>original: "śīla"</note>, which includes the practice of escorting and welcoming gurus. As a result of this, the wheel of movement appears on the soles of the feet. As a result of these, the marks appear on the palms of the two hands.

# The Explanation of the Noble Sutra of the Four Qualities

Homage to Manjushri in his youthful form.

Regarding the <term>sutra</term> <gloss>scriptural discourse</gloss> stating: A <term>bodhisattva</term> <gloss>awakening being</gloss>, a <term>mahasattva</term> <gloss>great being</gloss>, should not abandon these four qualities even at the cost of their life as long as they live. Why was this composed? It was composed to correctly teach those who are confused about the methods for attaining unsurpassed awakening after having entered the Great Vehicle. It is also to cause those who are heedless to correctly take them up, to encourage those who are discouraged, and to bring joy to those who have correctly entered the path.

Regarding application: one strives for the sake of one's own unsurpassed and perfect awakening, and for the sake of completely protecting all sentient beings from suffering.

Regarding realization: awakening is realized through two powers. What are the two? The power of intelligence and the power of diligence. One cannot realize awakening with ignorance or with little diligence.

Additionally, there are four qualities that harmonize with the accumulations of enlightenment, and because they form their basis, they are four.
